summary: This unit teaches you to work to the quality standards and procedures of a welding and fabrication workshop. You will learn what quality means, how to find and use the right drawings, specifications and procedures, how to check your measuring tools and measure against tolerances, and how to inspect your work before, during and after welding. You will also learn what to do with non-conforming work, how to keep honest records that make parts traceable, how to deal with a quality complaint, and how to help improve the way work is done.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Welding Level 2 qualification (MEM22423). It is about **quality**: making work that meets the drawing, the specification and the customer's needs, and proving that it does. Quality is not a separate job done by an inspector at the end; it is built into every step, from reading the drawing to handing over the finished part.

A gate that drags on its track, a bracket 5 mm too short, a stair rail with a cracked weld, a frame made from the wrong steel: each one costs time and money to put right, and some could hurt someone. A welder who works to the procedures, checks as they go and records honestly is worth more to any employer.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in the workshop
rows: Say what quality means in a fabrication shop and why it matters to the customer, the business and you.
Find and use the current job card, drawing, specification, WPS, procedures and checklists.
Choose, check and use measuring tools; decide whether a size is within tolerance.
Check, store and mark steel and consumables so that the right material is used and can be traced.
Check at every stage, before, during and after welding; respect hold points and first-off checks.
Tag, quarantine and report non-conforming work; tell a correction from a corrective action.
Fill in inspection records honestly and completely, so that work is traceable.
Deal professionally with a customer's complaint about quality.
Take part in continuous improvement, the PDCA cycle and 5S.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on quality, documents, tolerances, measuring tools, inspection, non-conforming work, corrective action, records, materials and continuous improvement.

A **written paper** with short answers (abbreviations and terms such as QMS, SOP, WPS, NCR, PDCA, 5S, calibration, title block, sampling and traceability, and simple tolerance sums) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Two group practicals.** In the first, you inspect a batch of 8 to 10 welded parts: check your measuring tools, measure the parts against the drawing, check squareness and weld sizes, look for surface faults, record and sign the results, tag and quarantine any faulty part, write a non-conformance report, and name the most common fault and a corrective action. In the second, you make a batch of L-shaped brackets from 6 mm flat bar to a drawing, with a quality checklist you write yourselves, a first-off check, a hold point after tacking, and self- and peer-inspection.

blocks.note: Learn the abbreviations. They are often asked as short answers, and they are all listed in the Revision section.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Quality** means meeting the customer's needs and the job's specification. It does not mean using the dearest materials or making everything shiny. A mild-steel gate made exactly to the drawing, primed and painted as agreed and delivered on the day promised is quality work; a beautifully ground gate that is 30 mm too narrow for the opening is not.

head: Quality point
What it means in the shop
rows: The grade, thickness and section the drawing calls for
Within the tolerances on the drawing; square, straight and in line
The right size and shape, fused into the parent metal, with no cracks and no other faults beyond what the specification allows
Grinding, priming and painting as specified; no sharp edges or spatter where they matter
Delivered when agreed, with the job card and inspection records complete

head: Who
Why it matters to them
rows: The product must be safe and must last. A failed weld on a stair rail, a balcony or a trailer can injure or kill.
Poor quality means scrap, rework, wasted time, repairs under warranty and lost customers. Good quality brings repeat work and a good name in the community.
Pride in your work, trust from your supervisor and customers, and better chances of a job or promotion; and less time spent fixing mistakes.

blocks.p: **Right first time** means doing the job correctly so that it needs no rework. Rework is expensive: the materials, the consumables and your time are paid for twice, and the customer waits. The later a fault is found, the more it costs. A wrong size found at cutting costs minutes; the same fault found after painting, or at the customer's house, costs hours, transport and the shop's good name.

blocks.note: Everyone on the job is responsible for quality: the person who cuts, the person who welds, the person who paints, and the inspector. You are responsible for the work you produce. The inspector checks it but cannot make it good.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Faulty work can fail in use and injure people, so safety and quality are closely linked. Rushing to catch up causes both poor work and accidents. Never skip a check, a procedure step or a piece of PPE to save time.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: Checking the product: measuring, inspecting and testing work to find faults
Planning and organising the work (procedures, training, checked tools, controlled documents) so that faults are prevented
The whole set of procedures, records and responsibilities a business uses to manage quality
An agreed document that sets out how something should be made, done or tested
A document that says exactly what the finished work must be
A set of steps that says how a task must be done; SOP stands for standard operating procedure
Detailed steps for one task at one workstation

blocks.p: Quality control finds faults after they happen; quality assurance tries to stop them happening. A good shop needs both.

ul: **ISO 9001** is the international standard for quality management systems. A business can be certified to it.
The **Bureau of Standards Jamaica (BSJ)** is Jamaica's national body that develops and promotes standards, and helps businesses to meet them.

Welding work is often done to a code, such as those of the American Welding Society (AWS), which sets rules for procedures, welder qualification and weld quality. Your instructor or supervisor will tell you which code or specification applies to each job.

blocks.p: A **WPS** is a written document that says how a particular weld must be made: the welding process, the parent metal and its thickness range, the joint design and preparation, the electrode or filler wire and its size, the current, polarity and voltage range, the shielding gas if any, the welding position, any pre-heat, and the number and order of runs. Follow it exactly. If you cannot (for example, the electrode it names is not in stock), stop and ask; do not substitute.

head: Document
What it tells you
rows: What the customer has asked for: job number, quantity, due date and special instructions
Shapes, sizes, tolerances, material, weld symbols and finish
The standard the finished work must meet: steel grade, weld size, finish, any tests
How each weld must be made
What must be checked, and where to record the results
How tasks such as storing electrodes, tagging faulty work or correcting records are done at the Centre

blocks.p: The **title block** is the box on a drawing, usually in the bottom right-hand corner, that shows its title, drawing number, scale, revision, date, units, material, general tolerances, and who drew and checked it.

head: In the title block
Why you check it
rows: It must match the number on the job card
You must have the latest issue
For example 1 : 10; work from the written sizes, never by measuring the paper
Applies to every size that has no tolerance of its own
The grade and size of steel to use

blocks.p: When a drawing is changed, it is given a new revision letter or number (for example Rev C becomes Rev D), and the change is noted in a revision table. A revision can change a size, a material, a hole, a weld or a finish. Old copies must be removed from the work area so that nobody works from wrong information. A **controlled copy** is one issued and tracked by the office or the supervisor; a photocopy, a photo on a phone or a sketch on the bench is not controlled.

flow: Check that the job number is the same on the job card, the drawing and the checklist
Check that the drawing's revision is the one the job card or master list names
Work only from controlled copies; hand old copies in to be removed
Read the whole drawing: sizes, tolerances, material, weld symbols and notes
If two documents disagree, or anything is unclear, stop and ask your supervisor before you start

blocks.note: Never choose a drawing because it is the cleanest copy or the one already on your bench. Use the current, controlled one, and if you are not sure which that is, ask.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: Nobody can make a part to exactly the size on the drawing. A **tolerance** is how far a size may be above or below the size given and still be accepted. The smallest size allowed is the **lower limit**; the largest is the **upper limit**. A size exactly on a limit is accepted.

blocks.note: Look for the general tolerance in the title block, for example "Unless stated otherwise: ± 2 mm". It applies to every size that has no tolerance of its own.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Tool
Used for
Typical smallest reading
rows: Checking that two faces or plates are at 90°
Angles and bevels, such as 45° or 30°
Small sizes: thickness, hole size, depth
Very small, precise sizes, using a thimble and a spindle
The leg length (and on some gauges the throat) of fillet welds
Reinforcement height, undercut depth, misalignment, bevel angle
Checking that work is level or plumb (upright)

blocks.p: Choose a tool that reads much finer than the tolerance. A tape that reads to 1 mm cannot tell you whether a size is within ± 0.2 mm; a caliper can.

blocks.h: Check the tool before you use it

flow: Choose a tool accurate enough for the tolerance
Look for damage: a bent rule, a kinked tape, a loose or bent hook, a dropped square, burred caliper jaws
Check that the calibration sticker or record is in date; if it is not, do not use the tool: report it and get one that is in date
Clean the jaws or faces; close a caliper and check that it reads zero; check a digital caliper's battery
If in doubt, check it against a known standard, such as a gauge block or a setting piece
After use, clean the tool and put it back in its case

blocks.p: **Calibration** is checking a measuring tool against a known, accurate standard and recording the result. Tools are calibrated at set intervals and labelled with the date of the next check.

ul: Measure on clean metal, with spatter and burrs removed.
Read the scale straight on, with your eye level with it, so that the reading is not shifted by your angle of view.
Hold the tape straight and hook it squarely; the sliding hook must be straight and move freely.

Check a rectangular frame for squareness with a try square at the corners and by comparing the two diagonals: once the opposite sides are the right length, the diagonals are equal only when the corners are square.
Write each reading down at once.
If two people get different readings, check the tools and the method, then measure again together; never just take the average or the reading that suits you.
Check every delivery against the purchase order and the drawing: grade, size (thickness, width, section) and quantity.
Check the mill certificate, if one is supplied, against the **heat number** stamped or painted on the steel. The heat number identifies the batch the steel was made in.
Look for damage: bends, deep pitting, heavy rust, cracks or layers in plate edges.
Wrong grade, wrong size, damaged or unmarked material: do not use it. Set it aside, label it, and report it.

blocks.p: Consumables have batch (lot) numbers too. Recording the heat and batch numbers used on a job means the materials can be traced if a problem is found later. This is called **traceability**.

head: Material
How to store it
Why
rows: On racks, off the ground, under cover, sorted by type, grade and size, with markings visible
Stops rust, bending and mix-ups, so the right material is used and can be traced
Marked with the grade (and heat number where records need it) before they go back on the rack
An unmarked offcut can end up in a job that needs a different grade
Once the packet is opened, in a heated holding oven at the temperature on the packet
Damp flux causes porosity and hydrogen cracking
In sealed packets, in a dry store, off the floor
Damp flux gives porosity and a poor arc
Sealed in its packing until used; spool covered on the machine; dry store
Rusty or damp wire feeds badly and causes porosity
Upright, chained, clearly labelled, valves closed, full and empty cylinders apart
The right gas is used, and cylinders are safe

ul: Use stock in date order, oldest first (first in, first out).
Handle finished work with care: use soft slings or packing so that painted or polished parts are not scratched or dented.
Never paint over or grind off a material marking.

blocks.note: Jamaica's humid air, the rainy seasons and salt air near the coast make rust and damp consumables a daily problem. Keep the electrode store closed, and never leave a box of low-hydrogen electrodes out on the bench overnight.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Inspect during the job, not only at the end, so that faults are found early, before more work and cost are added. The first and most common inspection on every weld is **visual inspection** by the welder.

head: Stage
What you check
rows: The right drawing (current revision) and the right material
Cut sizes and angles within tolerance
Joint preparation: bevel angle, root face, root gap
Settings match the WPS: process, electrode or wire, current, polarity, gas
Each run cleaned and checked before the next: slag, porosity, lack of fusion
Distortion: parts still square and in line
Weld size with a fillet gauge
Results written on the inspection record

blocks.h: Hold points, first-off checks and sampling

head: Term
Meaning
Example
rows: A stage where work must stop until it has been checked and released by a named person
After tacking, before full welding: the supervisor checks fit-up and squareness
Checking the first part made, fully, before making the rest
Check the first of 12 brackets against the drawing before cutting the other 11
Checking some items picked from a batch to judge the whole batch
Measure 1 part in every 10 from a batch of identical washers

blocks.note: Never work past a hold point because the person who must check is busy. Wait, do other work that is not held, and ask again. Do not ask someone else to sign in their place.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.h: What visual inspection can and cannot find

head: Visual inspection can usually find
It cannot find
rows: Undersize or oversize welds (with a gauge)
Cracks, porosity or slag inside the weld
Lack of fusion or penetration inside the joint, unless the root can be seen

blocks.p: Other tests find what the eye cannot. You will not do them at this level, but you should know they exist: **dye penetrant** (shows fine surface cracks), **magnetic particle** (cracks at or near the surface of steel), **ultrasonic** and **radiography** (X-ray) for faults inside the weld, and **bend** and **macro** tests on cut or bent test pieces.

blocks.h: Visible faults and what usually happens

head: Fault
What it looks like
Usual action (as the specification and supervisor decide)
rows: A groove melted into the plate along the toe
Check the depth against the specification; fill with another run if allowed
Weld metal lying on the plate without fusing
Grind out and re-weld; find the cause
A line in the weld or the plate
Always reject and report; grind out completely and re-weld only as instructed
Leg length smaller than the drawing
Small balls of metal; arc marks away from the joint
Clean off; report arc strikes on important work
A hollow at the end of a bead
Fill it; check for crater cracks
Parts out of line, out of square or bent
Report it; straighten only as instructed

blocks.note: Inspect after the slag and spatter are off, in good light. Look along the weld from both ends and from the side; a torch held low along the surface shows up undercut and porosity.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: **Non-conforming work** is work that does not meet the drawing, the specification or the procedure. Finding it is not a disaster; hiding it is.

flow: Stop work on the faulty part, so that you do not add more work and cost to it
Mark or tag it clearly as faulty, with a reject or hold tag
Move it to the quarantine area, so that nobody can use it by mistake
Tell your supervisor straight away: what is wrong, where, and how you found it
Record it on a non-conformance report (NCR) or the Centre's fault record
The supervisor decides what will happen to it
Carry out the decision and record what was done
Help to find the cause, so that it does not happen again

head: Decision
Meaning
rows: Fix the part so that it meets the drawing, then inspect it again
Accept it as it is, only with the written agreement of the customer or engineer
Throw it away, and record that it was scrapped
For faulty material or parts that were bought in

blocks.p: A **non-conformance report (NCR)** records the job number, the part, the drawing and its revision, what was required, what was found (the measured size or the fault), how many parts are affected, the date and your name. Later the decision, the action taken and a sign-off are added.

blocks.note: Never hide a fault, throw a faulty part in the scrap bin without telling anyone, or "fix" it without permission, for example by heating and stretching a short part or painting over a bad weld. Hidden faults reach customers and can hurt people.
blocks.label: Safety

blocks.h: Correction, corrective action and preventive action

head: Term
What it does
Example
rows: Fixes the fault that has already happened
Grind out a cracked tack on one frame and re-weld it
Finds and removes the cause, so that the fault does not happen again
A frame jig is found to be worn and out of square: it is repaired, and a weekly jig check is added to the procedure
Removes the cause of a possible fault before it happens
Before a new job starts, a jig is made so that the parts cannot be tacked out of square

blocks.p: The **root cause** is the real reason a fault happened. Keep asking "why?" until you reach something you can change. Example: brackets keep coming out 3 mm short.

ol: Why are they short? They were cut to the wrong length.
Why? The saw's length stop was set wrongly.
Why? It was set from a measurement taken with the end of a tape whose hook was bent.
Why was a damaged tape in use? Nobody checks the tapes, and there is no place to report damaged tools.
Root cause: no tool checks. Corrective action: check tools before each job and take damaged ones out of use; set the length stop from a checked rule.

blocks.p: After a corrective action, **check that it worked**, for example by measuring the next batch, and record both the correction and the corrective action.

ul: They show what was checked, by whom, when, and with what result.
They prove to the customer that the work meets the specification.
They make parts traceable if a problem is found later.
They help to spot faults that keep happening, so that the cause can be found.
They must be honest and accurate. A record that says a check was done when it was not is dangerous, because faulty work can reach the customer, and it is serious misconduct.

blocks.h: What a good inspection record contains

head: Item
Example
rows: Material and its heat or batch number
6 mm × 50 mm flat bar, heat number as stamped
E6013, 3.2 mm, batch number from the packet
Length, hole centres, squareness, weld leg length
Digital caliper No. 4, calibration in date
Name or signature, and the date
The inspector's name, signature and date

blocks.h: Correcting a mistake on a record

blocks.p: Strike the wrong entry through with **one line**, so that it can still be read, write the correct entry beside it, and initial (and date) the change. Never rub it out, use correction fluid, write over it or tear out the page.

**Traceability** means being able to follow a part back to its material batch, its welder and its inspection records. If a batch of electrodes is later found to be faulty, traceability shows exactly which jobs used it, so that only those need to be checked.
When you hand in the finished work, hand in the completed job card and inspection records with it. Return the drawings, label the parts, and leave the work area clean.

flow: Listen calmly and politely, and let the customer explain; do not argue or blame anyone
Thank them, and ask questions to understand exactly what is wrong and when it started
Record the details: name, phone number, job number, date, the problem
Do not promise what you are not allowed to give, such as a free replacement; say what will happen next and when
Pass it to your supervisor at once
The work is inspected against the drawing and the specification
If the fault is the shop's, it is put right as agreed, and the cause is found
The customer is contacted to check they are satisfied, and the complaint and the action are recorded

blocks.p: **Continuous improvement** means always looking for small ways to make the work better, safer, faster or cheaper, without lowering quality. Ideas can come from anyone, including trainees.

head: Stage
What happens
Example: brackets slow to clean
rows: Notice a problem, find its cause and plan a change
Spatter cleaning takes 15 minutes per bracket. The plates are rusty and the nozzle is clogged; plan to clean plates to bright metal and clear the nozzle every hour
Try the change on a small scale
Try it on one day's batch
Measure the results and compare them with before
Cleaning time drops to 5 minutes per bracket, and the welds still pass inspection
If it worked, make it the normal way and update the procedure; if not, try something else
Add the steps to the procedure and brief the team

ul: Pass your ideas to your supervisor so that they can be tried and agreed. Do not keep a good idea to yourself, and do not change a written procedure on your own.

Ideas a trainee might suggest: a simple jig to hold brackets square while tacking; a shadow board for gauges and clamps; a sign-in sheet on the electrode oven; marking every offcut before it goes back on the rack; a short checklist at each bench.

blocks.p: **5S** is a five-step system for organising a workplace so that it is clean, safe and efficient.

head: Step
Meaning
In the welding shop
rows: Scrap, broken tools and old drawings out of the bay
A shadow board for clamps, gauges and hand tools; labelled racks
Clean, and inspect while you clean
Sweep up slag and stubs; wipe the gauges; spot damaged leads
Make the first three steps the normal routine
A bay checklist at the end of each shift
Regular checks, with everyone taking part

blocks.p: Good housekeeping helps quality: tools and materials are found quickly and kept undamaged, the right gauge is used, and offcuts of different grades do not get mixed up.
Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain what quality means in a fabrication shop and why it matters to the customer, the business and me.
I can explain "right first time" and why faults found late cost the most.
I can tell quality control from quality assurance, and say what a QMS, an SOP and a WPS are.
I can name the documents for a job and make sure I am using the current, controlled ones.
I can read the title block of a drawing.
I can work out the limits of a tolerance and decide whether a size is acceptable.
I can choose the right measuring tool and check it for damage, zero and calibration before use.
I can check materials on delivery, store them correctly, and keep them traceable.
I can inspect my work before, during and after welding.
I can explain hold points, first-off checks and sampling.
I can say which faults visual inspection can and cannot find.
I can tag, quarantine and report non-conforming work, and fill in an NCR.
I can tell a correction from a corrective action, and help find a root cause.
I can fill in an inspection record honestly and correct a mistake on it properly.
I can deal professionally with a customer's complaint about quality.
I can explain continuous improvement, the PDCA cycle and 5S.

terms: BSJ
Bureau of Standards Jamaica, the national body that develops and promotes standards
Calibration
Checking a measuring tool against a known, accurate standard
Concession
Written agreement from the customer or engineer to accept a part that does not meet the drawing
Controlled copy
A copy of a document issued and tracked so that only the current version is in use
Correction
Fixing a fault that has already happened
Corrective action
Finding and removing the cause of a fault so that it does not happen again
First-off check
Checking the first part made before making the rest
Heat number
The number that identifies the batch steel was made in
Hold point
A stage where work must stop until it has been checked and released
Non-conforming work
Work that does not meet the drawing, specification or procedure
NCR
Non-conformance report: the record of a fault and what was done about it
PDCA
Plan, Do, Check, Act: a cycle for improving work
QA
Quality assurance: planning work so that faults are prevented
QC
Quality control: checking the product to find faults
QMS
Quality management system: the procedures, records and responsibilities for quality
Quarantine
Keeping faulty or doubtful items apart, tagged, so that they are not used by mistake
Revision
A new issue of a drawing or document, shown by a letter or number
Right first time
Doing the job correctly so that it needs no rework
Root cause
The real reason a fault happened
Sampling
Checking some items from a batch to judge the whole batch
SOP
Standard operating procedure: the set steps for doing a task
Specification
A document that says exactly what the finished work must be
Title block
The box on a drawing showing its title, number, scale, revision and other details
Tolerance
How far a size may be above or below the size given
Traceability
Being able to follow a part back to its material, its welder and its records
WPS
Welding procedure specification: how a particular weld must be made
5S
Sort, Set in order, Shine, Standardise, Sustain

c1.title: Handrail brackets for a school in Chapelton
c1.text: Davian is making 24 handrail brackets for a school in Chapelton, Clarendon. The job card calls for drawing HR-07 Rev D. On his bench is a copy marked Rev C; the office file holds a copy marked Rev D. The drawing gives the bracket length as 180 ± 1.5 mm and the bolt holes as 14 +0.5 / −0 mm. The supervisor, Miss Dixon, has set a hold point after tacking.

c2.title: Checking the tools in Lionel Town
c2.text: Stacy-Ann and Omari, trainees at a fabrication shop in Lionel Town, Clarendon, are inspecting base plates drawn as 250 ± 1 mm square. Stacy-Ann's digital caliper reads 0.12 mm with its jaws closed. The hook on Omari's tape measure is bent outwards. The shop has no try square big enough for the plates.

c3.title: Undersize fillet welds in Highgate
c3.text: A shop in Highgate, St Mary, makes steel frames for market stalls. The drawing calls for 6 mm fillet welds, but the customer's inspector has found many welds with legs of only 4 to 5 mm. Garfield, a trainee, notices that the fillet gauge the welders share has a chipped edge and no calibration label, and that a new welder was never shown how to read the drawing's weld symbols. The undersize welds found so far are being built up with an extra run.

c4.title: A steel delivery in Annotto Bay
c4.text: Yanique receives a delivery of five sheets of 8 mm plate at a shop in Annotto Bay, St Mary. Four sheets are stamped with the grade and a heat number; one sheet has no marking at all, and the mill certificate lists only four heat numbers. Some offcuts on the shop's rack are also unmarked.

c5.title: Rusting stair rails at a guest house in Brown's Town
c5.text: Mrs Facey, who runs a guest house in Brown's Town, St Ann, emails the shop that made her steel stair rails six weeks ago: there are rust streaks at several welds and the paint is lifting. The job card says the rails were to be wire-brushed, primed and given two top coats. Kirk, a junior welder who helped make them, opens the email first.

questions.q: Which drawing should Davian work from?
o: Rev C, since it is the copy that was left on his bench for him
Rev D from the office, handing the Rev C copy in to be removed
Rev C, until Miss Dixon tells him in person that Rev D applies
Either one, since a new revision only changes the title block
questions.why: The job card names Rev D, and the office file holds the controlled copy. The out-of-date copy on the bench must be handed in so that nobody works from wrong information; a revision can change sizes, holes, materials or welds.

questions.q: Davian measures four brackets: 178.4 mm, 181.5 mm, 179.0 mm and 181.6 mm. Which are within tolerance?
o: 181.5 mm and 179.0 mm only
179.0 mm only
All four, as each is within 2 mm of 180
questions.why: 180 ± 1.5 mm allows 178.5 mm to 181.5 mm, and a size exactly on a limit is accepted. 178.4 mm is 0.1 mm too short and 181.6 mm is 0.1 mm too long.

questions.q: The bolt holes have been drilled at 13.9 mm. What should Davian conclude?
o: They are fine, as 0.1 mm is too small to matter on a bracket
They are undersize and non-conforming, as no minus is allowed
They are fine, as the tolerance allows 0.5 mm either way
They are oversize, and must be welded up and drilled again
questions.why: 14 +0.5 / −0 mm means the hole may be up to 0.5 mm bigger (14.0 to 14.5 mm) but not smaller. At 13.9 mm the holes are undersize, so the brackets are non-conforming until they are put right, for example by opening the holes to size.

questions.q: Davian has tacked his first bracket. What should happen before he tacks the other 23?
o: Full welding of the first bracket, to see how it turns out
A check of the last bracket once all 24 have been made
A first-off check of that bracket against the drawing
Painting of the first bracket so its finish can be judged
questions.why: Checking the first part fully before making the rest catches a wrong setting, template or reading while only one part is affected; finding it at the end could mean 24 faulty brackets.

questions.q: At the hold point, Miss Dixon is tied up with a delivery for an hour. What should Davian do?
o: Wait for her check, and meanwhile cut and clean the next parts
Weld out the brackets, since he has already checked them himself
Ask another trainee to check them and sign in place of Miss Dixon
Weld out one bracket so that she can check a finished example
questions.why: A hold point means work stops until the named person has checked and released it. Working past it, or getting someone else to sign, defeats the check; use the time for work that is not held.

questions.q: Stacy-Ann's caliper reads 0.12 mm with its jaws closed. What should she do?
o: Take 0.12 mm off every reading in her head as she goes
Carry on, since 0.12 mm is small beside a ± 1 mm tolerance
Add 0.12 mm to each reading to be sure that the plates pass
Clean it, re-zero it, and report it if it will not hold zero
questions.why: Dirt or spatter between the jaws often causes a false zero. Clean, close and zero the caliper before use; a tool that will not hold zero is faulty and must be reported, not corrected in your head.

questions.q: Why does the bent hook on Omari's tape matter?
o: Every reading from the hook may be out by 1 mm or more
The tape will read wrongly only on lengths of over a metre
A bent hook matters only when measuring inside a frame
It does not matter, as a tape can be read from either end
questions.why: The sliding hook is made so that inside and outside measurements both start from true zero. If it is bent or loose, every reading taken from it is wrong, so the tape must be taken out of use and reported.

questions.q: With no large square, how can Stacy-Ann and Omari check that a plate is truly square?
o: Measure all four sides and check that they are equal
Measure both diagonals and check that they are equal
Check one corner with the fillet weld gauge
Lay a spirit level across the plate both ways
questions.why: A shape with four equal sides can still lean over like a diamond. A rectangle or square has 90° corners only when its two diagonals are equal as well.

questions.q: Building up each undersize weld with an extra run is an example of what?
o: A corrective action
A preventive action
A correction
A concession
questions.why: A correction fixes a fault that has already happened, here one weld at a time. It does nothing to stop the next weld being undersize; that needs a corrective action on the cause.

questions.q: Which of these is a corrective action for the undersize welds?
o: Add an extra run to each undersize weld the inspector found
Ask the inspector to accept 5 mm legs on all future frames
Replace the damaged gauge and train welders on weld symbols
Paint the frames at once so that weld sizes are harder to see
questions.why: A corrective action removes the causes so that the fault stops: a damaged gauge gives false readings, and a welder who cannot read the symbol cannot weld to it. Building up welds is only a correction, and hiding faults is never acceptable.

questions.q: How should the shop check that its corrective action has worked?
o: Gauge the welds on the next frames and record the results
Assume it has worked, since the gauge and the training are new
Wait to see whether the customer complains again next month
Ask the new welder whether he feels more confident now
questions.why: The Check step means measuring the results. If the next frames' welds gauge at 6 mm or more, the action worked; if not, there is another cause to find. Feelings and waiting for complaints prove nothing.

questions.q: What should happen to frames already welded that have not yet been gauged?
o: Send them out, since only some welds were undersize
Scrap them all, since some were undersize before
Check only the frames welded by the new welder
Tag and hold them until each weld has been checked
questions.why: Every frame welded while the gauge was damaged is suspect, whoever welded it. Holding and checking each one stops faulty work reaching the customer without scrapping good frames.

questions.q: What is the problem with the sheet that has no marking?
o: Its grade cannot be proved or traced, so it must not be used
None: it came in the same delivery, so it is the same steel
It can be used, but only on jobs that will be painted
It can be used once someone paints the right grade on it
questions.why: Without a marking or a certificate, nobody can show what the steel is. Set it aside, label it and report it; painting a grade on it would be a false record.

questions.q: What should be done with offcuts before they go back on the rack?
o: Sort them by length only, with the longest at the top
Keep them on the floor, well apart from the new stock
Paint them all one colour so that the rack looks tidy
Mark each with its grade so that it can be identified
questions.why: An unmarked offcut can end up in a job that needs a different grade. Marking the grade, and the heat number where records need it, keeps offcuts usable and traceable; steel kept on the floor rusts.

questions.q: Before signing the delivery note, what should Yanique check the sheets against?
o: The delivery driver's word that it is the right steel
The price on last month's invoice from the supplier
The purchase order and the drawing's material list
The total weight printed on the delivery docket
questions.why: Goods are checked against what was ordered and what the job needs: grade, size and quantity, with markings and certificates. Signing first means accepting whatever came, including wrong or unmarked steel.

questions.q: What should Kirk do with Mrs Facey's email?
o: Reply that the paint was fine when the rails left the shop
Promise her a free new set of rails by the end of next week
Pass it to his supervisor at once, with the job number
Delete it, since the guest house has already paid in full
questions.why: Complaints go to the supervisor quickly, with the details, so that the work can be inspected against the job card. A junior worker should not argue, admit blame or promise a replacement he cannot authorise.

questions.q: Which record would best show whether the rails were finished as the job card required?
o: The receipt for the steel that was bought for the job
The inspection record signed at the painting stage
The delivery note from the paint supplier for the job
The shop's attendance register for the weeks of the job
questions.why: A signed inspection record at the finishing stage shows what was checked, by whom and when. Without it, nobody can show that the rails were cleaned, primed and painted as specified.

questions.q: The inspection finds that the rails were never primed. Which response deals with the cause?
o: Repaint Mrs Facey's rails with two thicker top coats
Tell the painters to work faster to catch up on orders
Use a dearer brand of top coat on all rails from now on
Add a signed priming check to the finishing checklist
questions.why: Re-doing her rails properly (cleaned, primed, painted) is the correction. The corrective action makes priming hard to miss again, such as a signed check or a hold point before top coats; a dearer top coat does not replace a missing primer.

questions.q: Which of these is quality assurance rather than quality control?
o: Measuring each finished bracket against the drawing
Checking weld sizes with a fillet gauge after welding
Picking 1 part in 10 from a batch to inspect it
Training welders on the procedure before a new job
questions.why: Quality assurance plans and organises the work so that faults are prevented: procedures, training, checked tools. Measuring, gauging and sampling finished work are quality control: they check the product.

questions.q: A shop writes its clearing, tidying and cleaning steps into one checklist that every bay follows at the end of each shift. Which step of 5S is this?
o: Sort
Standardise
Set in order
Shine
questions.why: Standardise makes Sort, Set in order and Shine part of the normal routine, usually with a written checklist or schedule. Sort removes what is not needed, Set in order gives everything a marked place, and Shine is cleaning while checking for damage.
